But you know from Shock II what the grand tests keyed, twice, and what you chose instead. When levosimendan is offered, it's levosimendan. Milrinone only if levosimendan isn't there.

One mechanism question belongs here. A drug that raises cardiac output, dilates veins and speeds calcium reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Half the candidates chose selective beta-one stimulation or troponin C sensitisation. It's phosphodiesterase three inhibition: milrinone. The reuptake is the clue. That's cyclic AMP at work, and levosimendan doesn't raise it.

And the balloon pump. Not routinely. You have the class from the last card.

So far the shock has come from the left ventricle. There's one infarct where it comes from the right, and there almost everything you'd reach for is wrong.

steps.bridge: Rhythm, failure and shock are done. The third family is structural: the infarct tears.

lesson.text:
An inferior STEMI. Pressure eighty over fifty. The lungs are clear and the neck veins are full. Hypotension with dry lungs and a high venous pressure: the left ventricle isn't the problem. It's the right.

The right coronary artery supplies the right ventricle, and when it's blocked near its origin the right ventricle infarcts along with the inferior wall. You confirm it with a right-sided ECG: ST elevation of one millimetre or more in V4R. Record it early, because that sign fades within hours.

You met the physiology in the first hour, with the nitrate. A stunned right ventricle is a passive conduit. It moves blood to the left side only if it's filled at a high pressure. So the treatment is the reverse of left-sided shock.

First, fluid. A cautious crystalloid bolus while primary PCI is arranged. Cautious, because the two ventricles share a septum and a pericardium. Overfill the right, and the septum bulges into the left and the output falls again.

Second, avoid everything that lowers preload.

[[Right ventricular infarct: clear lungs, raised JVP, hypotension, ST elevation in V4R. Give fluid. Avoid nitrates, diuretics, morphine and beta-blockers.]]

Third, if fluid fails, dobutamine. And protect the atrial kick. Inferior infarcts cause AV block, as you've just learned, and a right ventricle that depends on filling loses a great deal when the atria stop contributing. So if you pace, pace both chambers in sequence.

The bank stem is the one from the first hour, and it's worth hearing again now that you have the whole picture. Inferior STEMI, given aspirin, nitrate and morphine. The pressure falls from one hundred and sixty over ninety to sixty over thirty. Half called it a drug reaction. It's cardiogenic shock from a right ventricular infarct, and two of those three drugs caused the fall.

The discriminator is the lungs. Shock with crackles is the left ventricle: no fluid. Shock with clear lungs and full neck veins after an inferior infarct is the right ventricle: fluid.

That's the rhythm and the pump. One family of complications is left, and it's the one where minutes matter most.

spine: AIVR at reperfusion: wide, regular, near sinus rate; benign, no treatment. VT: electrolytes (K ≥4, Mg), cardiovert if unstable, β-blocker or amiodarone if stable.
Mechanism by timing: early VF re-entry; AIVR enhanced normal automaticity; 24–72 h VT/NSVT ABNORMAL automaticity; weeks–years scar re-entry.
AV block: inferior MI → nodal, narrow escape, atropine works, transient. Anterior MI → infranodal, wide escape, needs pacing. Inferior MI causes more block of every degree.
Killip I–IV: none; S3/crackles <50%; pulmonary oedema; shock. High BP oedema → nitrate + NIV. Low BP → norepinephrine, then dobutamine.
STEMI shock: immediate culprit-only PCI (I), transfer whatever the delay. Routine IABP class III; IABP for a mechanical complication IIa.
RV infarct: inferior STEMI, clear lungs, raised JVP, V4R. Fluid; no nitrates, diuretics, morphine, β-blockers; keep AV synchrony.

questions.text: Ruptures, aneurysm and the long road after

open.text:
The last section begins with the worst days and ends with the rest of the patient's life.

Dead muscle is soft. For the first week, before scar forms, it can tear, and where it tears decides what you see. The bank has asked six questions on that.

[[Three ruptures in the first week: free wall gives tamponade, septum gives a shunt with a loud murmur, papillary muscle gives acute mitral regurgitation. All three end in surgery.]]

If the wall holds but never recovers, it thins and bulges, and that's the aneurysm. Then come the drugs every survivor takes home, which is where your other missed question sits: the ACE inhibitor after an infarct with an ejection fraction of thirty-two per cent.

Listen for one trap above the others. In the rupture questions the examiner asks for the next step, and offers norepinephrine, a balloon pump and surgery side by side. The balloon pump that is class three in routine shock is the right answer here, because a mechanical complication is the exception.

Start with the three tears, side by side.

steps.bridge: Of the three, the septal rupture forces the hardest decision: operate now or wait.

lesson.text:
Take each rupture from its mechanism, and the presentation follows.

The free wall. The ventricle opens into the pericardium, and the sac fills in moments. The heart keeps its electrical rhythm but can't fill, so there's no output. Sudden chest pain, collapse, a rhythm on the monitor and no pulse. The finding is blood in the pericardium with tamponade. Two grand-test stems gave sudden hypotension or pulseless electrical activity days after a large STEMI with tamponade on echo. The answer both times: free wall rupture. It's rare, under one per cent, and the risks are older age, no reperfusion and late lysis.

The septum. Now the hole is between the ventricles, and blood takes the easy path, left to right. The lungs are flooded and the body is starved, so you get rapid heart failure and shock, in the first week. The sign is a new, loud systolic murmur, often with a thrill at the left sternal edge. And if you sample the blood, the oxygen saturation steps up between the right atrium and the pulmonary artery.

The papillary muscle. The mitral leaflet loses its anchor and flails, and the ventricle empties backwards into a small left atrium that has had no time to stretch. Sudden pulmonary oedema, with or without shock. Which muscle? The posteromedial one, because it has a single blood supply, from the posterior descending artery. The anterolateral muscle has two. So this follows an inferior or posterior infarct, often a small one.

And here's the catch. The murmur may be soft or short, because the left atrial pressure rises so fast that the gradient disappears. A quiet heart with flash pulmonary oedema still needs an echo.

{{ | **Free wall** | **Septum** | **Papillary muscle**
Presents | collapse, PEA | failure / shock, days 1–7 | flash pulmonary oedema
Finding | tamponade | loud murmur, O₂ step-up | soft murmur, flail leaflet
Bridge | pericardiocentesis | IABP | IABP, vasodilator
Then | surgical repair | surgery / device closure | mitral surgery}}

[[Septal rupture: loud murmur at the left sternal edge with an oxygen step-up. Papillary muscle rupture: apical murmur, often soft, with flash pulmonary oedema, after an inferior infarct.]]

Now the management, where four of the six questions sit.

All three end in surgery. The question is what you do in the minutes before. For the free wall, pericardiocentesis buys time. For the other two, think about where the blood is going. It has two exits: forward into the aorta, or the wrong way, through the hole or the valve. How much goes each way depends on the resistance of each exit. Lower the resistance in the aorta, and more goes forward.

That's what the balloon pump does. It deflates just before systole and drops the afterload, and it raises the diastolic pressure that feeds the coronaries. A vasopressor does the opposite. It raises the afterload and drives more blood the wrong way.

[[For shock from papillary muscle or septal rupture, the bridge to surgery is the balloon pump, which lowers afterload. Norepinephrine raises afterload and worsens the leak.]]

Here's how the bank played it. An inferior STEMI with a murmur, pulmonary oedema, cold and hypotensive: which intervention? Only thirty-eight per cent chose the balloon pump; most chose norepinephrine. Papillary rupture on echo with flash pulmonary oedema: next step? The balloon pump again, and fewer than half chose it, because valve replacement was sitting beside it. When the stem says next and the balloon is offered, stabilise first. But in a third stem, partial rupture with hypotension, there was no balloon option, and the choices were diuretics and observe, a vasodilator and reassess in forty-eight hours, or urgent mitral surgery. Then it's surgery.

One more, simpler. A posterior infarct, then breathlessness with a new apical holosystolic murmur and crackles. The mechanism is acute mitral regurgitation. Not pulmonary embolism, and not pump failure.

Last, the mortality figures on the card. Free wall rupture, seventy-five to eighty per cent. Papillary muscle, twenty to twenty-five per cent with surgery. For the septum the card says twenty to forty per cent with early surgery. That's optimistic, and the next card tells you why.

steps.bridge: The wall that tears kills quickly. The wall that holds but never recovers causes a slower problem.

lesson.text:
The septal rupture gets a card of its own because of one decision: when to operate. It hasn't been asked, so take the logic and two corrections.

First, where it happens. An anterior infarct tears the septum near the apex, usually a simple hole. An inferior infarct tears it at the base, a more complex defect that does worse. The card says anterior or posterolateral, following its notes. The usual pairing is anterior and inferior, and that's the one to learn.

Now the timing, which is a real dilemma. Operate early, and the surgeon is sewing a patch into dead muscle that holds stitches badly. Wait a few weeks, and the edges turn to scar and the repair holds. But while you wait the hole can enlarge, and the patient can die.

So the patient decides.

[[Septal rupture: refractory shock means surgery now, despite the risk. A patient who stabilises on support can have delayed repair once the edges have scarred.]]

The trap is the blanket rule: wait four to six weeks for every septal rupture. Only for the stable.

The second correction is the number. The card gives twenty to forty per cent mortality for early surgery. In the large surgical registry it was about fifty-four per cent for repair within seven days, and eighteen per cent after that.

And the newer option: percutaneous closure with a device, in selected anatomy.

steps.bridge: The structure is dealt with. What remains is the prescription for life, and one of your misses is in it.

lesson.text:
Suppose the wall doesn't tear. A large infarct that goes right through the wall and isn't reperfused in time heals as a thin sheet of scar, and with every beat that sheet bulges outward. That's a left ventricular aneurysm. It follows fewer than five in a hundred infarcts, fewer still since primary PCI, and it sits where the big anterior infarcts are: the anteroseptal wall and the apex.

The ECG has two features, and together they're the question. Q waves, because the muscle is dead. And ST elevation that never comes down.

[[ST elevation that persists for weeks after an anterior infarct, with Q waves, no new pain and no rise in troponin, is a left ventricular aneurysm, not a new infarct.]]

The trap is to call it re-infarction and send the patient for reperfusion.

That fits into a simple three-way reading of an ECG, which a DocT question tested. Q waves with no ST elevation: an old, healed infarct. ST elevation with symptoms or a rising troponin: an acute one. Q waves with persistent ST elevation weeks later: an aneurysm. The stem gave a patient with known coronary disease, fatigue, and Q waves in leads one, aVL and V5. Fewer than half said old lateral infarction. The rest said acute coronary syndrome. But Q waves are permanent. Acute ischaemia needs ST or T wave change and a story to match.

The main complication comes from stasis. Blood sits still in a pouch that doesn't contract, a thrombus forms at the apex, and pieces travel to the brain and the limbs. The card says long-term oral anticoagulation, and that's the classic exam answer. The current European guideline is more modest: anticoagulation should be considered for three to six months, guided by repeat imaging.

Surgery is for a large aneurysm, recurrent embolism, or one causing refractory heart failure or ventricular arrhythmias.

And one mimic that matters. A true aneurysm has a wide neck, its wall is scar, and it rarely ruptures. A pseudoaneurysm is a free wall rupture that the pericardium has sealed off. Its neck is narrow, its wall isn't myocardium at all, and it does rupture. So it goes to the surgeon.

steps.bridge: The beta-blocker row has a soft cell: LVEF above 40%. Four recent trials tested exactly that.

lesson.text:
The patient is going home. Which drugs go with him, and which of them actually lengthen his life? This card is a grid, and the column that matters is the ejection fraction.

Start with the damaged ventricle: an ejection fraction of forty per cent or less, or heart failure.

After a large infarct the surviving muscle is overloaded. The body's answer is to switch on angiotensin and catecholamines, and over months they make the ventricle dilate and scar. That's remodelling, and it's what kills later. So the drugs that prolong life are the ones that block those signals.

The ACE inhibitor blocks angiotensin and limits the dilatation. Class one.

That's the grand-test question you missed. An infarct, an ejection fraction of thirty-two per cent, and the question was which drug to continue long term for secondary prevention. The key was the ACE inhibitor. It isn't there for the blood pressure. It's there for the ventricle.

[[After an infarct with an LVEF of forty per cent or less, an ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker are both class one, long term. Add a mineralocorticoid antagonist if there is also heart failure or diabetes.]]

The beta-blocker blocks the catecholamines. It lowers oxygen demand, raises the threshold for ventricular fibrillation, and in the older trials cut deaths by more than a fifth. Class one.

The mineralocorticoid antagonist is the third. Aldosterone keeps driving fibrosis even on an ACE inhibitor. In the EPHESUS trial eplerenone reduced deaths in exactly this group: an ejection fraction of forty or less with heart failure or diabetes. Check the potassium and creatinine first. The card grades it one B; the twenty twenty-three guideline has it at one A.

Now the other column, an ejection fraction above forty. The ACE inhibitor drops to class two a, unless there is diabetes, hypertension or kidney disease, which keep it at class one. So does the beta-blocker, and the next card is about how soft that has become.

Two rows don't change with the ejection fraction. A high-dose statin for everyone, class one. And dual antiplatelet therapy for twelve months.

{{**Drug** | **LVEF ≤40% or HF** | **LVEF >40%**
β-blocker | **I** | IIa
ACE inhibitor | **I** | IIa (I if DM, HTN, CKD)
MRA | **I** (with HF or diabetes) | –
High-dose statin | I | I
DAPT | 12 months | 12 months}}

A DocT question shows the trap. After an infarct, an ejection fraction of twenty-five per cent, stable but breathless: which therapy improves long-term prognosis? The options were a beta-blocker, intravenous milrinone, digoxin and nitrates. Fewer than half chose the beta-blocker. Sort them by one question: does it prolong life, or only ease symptoms? Milrinone raises oxygen demand and arrhythmias and worsens long-term survival; it's a bridge in shock. Digoxin reduced admissions but not deaths. Nitrates treat angina.

[[Drugs that prolong life after an infarct with a low ejection fraction: beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, mineralocorticoid antagonist, statin. Inotropes, digoxin, nitrates and diuretics treat symptoms only.]]

steps.bridge: One card left: the 2025 American targets for lipids, rehabilitation and haemoglobin.

lesson.text:
The beta-blocker earned its place before stents, when infarcts were large and ventricles were left damaged. Does it still help a patient whose artery was opened within the hour and whose ventricle is normal? Recent trials asked, and the answer depends on the ejection fraction. This hasn't been asked in the bank, but it's new enough to appear.

REDUCE-AMI. Ejection fraction fifty per cent or more. No benefit.

REBOOT. Ejection fraction above forty, no heart failure. No benefit overall.

BETAMI-DANBLOCK. Ejection fraction forty or more. Fewer events, fourteen point two per cent against sixteen point three, mainly fewer new infarctions.

Why the disagreement? The signal sat in the patients with a mildly reduced ejection fraction, between forty and forty-nine. Pooled across the trials, nearly nineteen hundred of them, death, infarction or heart failure fell from fourteen point four per cent to ten point seven. A quarter fewer.

[[Beta-blocker after infarction: clear benefit with an LVEF of forty or below, benefit in the pooled data at forty to forty-nine, and no demonstrated benefit at fifty or above.]]

The mechanism explains it. The drug protects a damaged ventricle from arrhythmia and remodelling. Where there's little damage, there's little to protect.

One caution. Both guidelines were written before most of these trials reported, and both still support a beta-blocker after an infarct. So for the exam it is not a wrong answer. What's wrong is the statement that it improves outcome in every patient.

The last card is the discharge checklist from the American guideline of twenty twenty-five. None of it has been asked yet, so learn the numbers and one exception.

A high-intensity statin for everyone, whatever the starting cholesterol. Then the LDL on that statin decides whether you add a second agent, such as ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor.

[[American guideline, twenty twenty-five: on a maximal statin, an LDL of seventy milligrams per decilitre or more means add a non-statin agent, class one. Between fifty-five and sixty-nine, adding one is reasonable, class two a.]]

The trap is an LDL of sixty with ezetimibe called class one. Recheck a fasting lipid panel four to eight weeks after any change. And refer for cardiac rehabilitation before discharge, class one, because patients referred later often never go.

Now the exception, and for an intensivist it's the most interesting line in the packet. You transfuse at a haemoglobin of seven. That threshold was never tested in acute infarction, where the muscle beyond a narrowed artery depends on every gram. The MINT trial tested it, and a liberal target of ten gave fewer deaths or infarctions than a restrictive one, narrowly missing significance.

[[In acute coronary syndrome with anaemia and no active bleeding, transfusing to keep the haemoglobin at ten grams per decilitre may be reasonable. That is class two b, and an exception to the general threshold of seven.]]

That's the infarct, start to finish. You recognised it, opened the artery, covered it with the right drugs, managed what went wrong, and sent the patient home.

But look at what he takes with him. A scar, and around it muscle that was ischaemic. You saw in this packet what those do: the scar is a circuit for re-entry, and injured cells fire when they shouldn't. Nearly every arrhythmia you'll meet on the unit begins in one of those two places. So that's next: a monitor, a rhythm that's too fast or too slow, and how to read it.

spine: Days 1–7, necrotic muscle tears. Free wall → haemopericardium, tamponade, PEA. Septum → loud murmur, O₂ step-up, shock. Papillary (posteromedial, inferior MI) → flash pulmonary oedema, soft murmur.
All three need surgery. Bridge for septal/papillary rupture = IABP (lowers afterload, IIa); norepinephrine worsens the leak. No IABP option → urgent surgery.
VSR: refractory shock → operate now; stable on support → delayed repair. Registry mortality ~54% within 7 days.
Aneurysm: persistent ST elevation + Q waves weeks later, no troponin rise; apical thrombus → anticoagulate (ESC 3–6 months). Pseudoaneurysm: narrow neck, ruptures, surgery.
LVEF ≤40%: β-blocker, ACE inhibitor (class I), MRA if HF/diabetes; statin and 12-month DAPT for all. Inotropes, digoxin, nitrates do not prolong life.
β-blocker with LVEF ≥50%: no proven benefit (REDUCE-AMI, REBOOT). LDL ≥70 on statin → add non-statin (1). Hb 10 in ACS anaemia may be reasonable (MINT).

close.text:
So let's walk back through Patient C, from the door to discharge.

You read his ECG in ten minutes, put him on a monitor, and held the oxygen because his saturation was fine. You chose the road by the clock. You covered the artery with drugs that stop platelets and drugs that stop thrombin, and you learned which of them to hold, and when. You watched for the rhythms and the failing pump that follow an infarct. And you sent him home on the drugs that keep the scar from growing.

Now the traps. These are the ones you've actually met.

One. The PCI centre is far away. The tempting cut-off is ninety minutes. [[The choice between primary PCI and lysis is made at one hundred and twenty minutes, from diagnosis to wire. Beyond that, lyse within ten minutes, then transfer.]]

Two. An NSTEMI, anatomy not yet known. The tempting move is to load prasugrel now. Don't. If he's going for early angiography, the P2Y12 inhibitor waits for the anatomy, because he may need bypass surgery instead. You missed this one.

Three. Creatinine clearance of twenty-four. The tempting answer is that enoxaparin is contraindicated. [[Below a clearance of thirty, enoxaparin is not stopped. It's given once a day instead of twice.]] Another grand-test miss.

Four. Urgent bypass surgery, and he's on eptifibatide. The short-acting glycoprotein inhibitors are stopped only two to four hours before. Clopidogrel and ticagrelor need at least a day.

Five. Discharge, and his ejection fraction is thirty-two percent. The ACE inhibitor is a class one drug at forty percent or below, together with a beta-blocker. That was a miss too.

And six. Saturation ninety-five, and someone puts him on two litres of oxygen. Routine oxygen above ninety percent is class three. It doesn't help, and it may harm.

The check comes up on the next screen. Answer each in your head before you tap it open.

And carry one picture into the next packet. Patient C goes home with a scar, and around it, muscle that was starved. Those are the places where rhythms go wrong. So next, the monitor shows you a rhythm that's too fast, or too slow. How do you read it?

drill.q: STEMI, nearest PCI centre 150 km (or 4 h) away. Next step?
drill.a: Thrombolysis within 10 min, then transfer. PCI is chosen only if the wire can cross within 120 min of diagnosis (NEET 2025, Marrow, DocT).

drill.q: What do 120, 60 and 90 minutes each mean in STEMI?
drill.a: 120: choose PCI over lysis. 60: target at a PCI centre. 90: target if transferred.

drill.q: After lysis: when is it judged, what defines failure, and what follows success?
drill.a: At 60-90 min. Failure = <50% ST resolution, ongoing pain or instability → rescue PCI now. Success → angiography at 2-24 h.

drill.q: DES 2 months ago, sudden anterior ST elevation. Management?
drill.a: Stent thrombosis = STEMI: DAPT, anticoagulation, urgent PCI. Not lysis, nitrates, echo or observation (NEET 2025; DocT GT 48%).

drill.q: STEMI in cardiogenic shock, PCI centre 3.5 h away: lyse or transfer?
drill.a: Transfer for revascularisation whatever the delay; culprit-only PCI (9% right).

drill.q: SaO₂ 95% in ACS: oxygen?
drill.a: Withhold. Oxygen only if SaO₂ <90% or PaO₂ <60 mmHg; routine oxygen above that is class III (DETO2X-AMI).

drill.q: Inferior STEMI: BP falls to 60/30 ten minutes after nitroglycerin. Diagnosis and treatment?
drill.a: RV infarct (cardiogenic shock), not a drug reaction. Fluid bolus, V4R, no nitrates, diuretics or morphine.

drill.q: Absolute contraindication to lysis: SBP >180, warfarin, TIA 3 months ago, or previous haemorrhagic stroke?
drill.a: Previous haemorrhagic stroke (absolute, for life). The rest are relative. Ischaemic stroke <6 months is absolute; a known AVM is absolute on every list.

drill.q: Tenecteplase: dose for 72 kg aged 60, and aged 80? Which P2Y12 inhibitor with it?
drill.a: 40 mg single bolus; 20 mg (half dose at ≥75 y). Clopidogrel 300 mg (75 mg, no load, if >75 y).

drill.q: Recent stent on aspirin + clopidogrel, needs urgent surgery. IV bridge?
drill.a: Cangrelor: the only IV P2Y12 inhibitor, t½ 3-6 min. Not tirofiban or eptifibatide (GP IIb/IIIa).

drill.q: Breathless 12 h after PCI; SpO₂, examination, ECG and CT normal. Culprit drug and mechanism?
drill.a: Ticagrelor: adenosine accumulation. Usually mild and self-limiting (30% right).

drill.q: ACS with a recent TIA going for PCI: which P2Y12 inhibitor is contraindicated?
drill.a: Prasugrel (prior stroke or TIA).

drill.q: NSTEMI for early angiography, anatomy unknown: give a P2Y12 inhibitor now?
drill.a: No. Routine pretreatment is class III; defer to PCI (GT7 Q104). Aspirin yes.

drill.q: NSTE-ACS anticoagulant: angiography <24 h vs >24 h?
drill.a: <24 h: UFH (enoxaparin IIa). >24 h: fondaparinux (OASIS-5: half the major bleeding of enoxaparin). Fondaparinux alone in primary PCI: class III.

drill.q: NSTE-ACS, CrCl 24 mL/min: enoxaparin?
drill.a: 1 mg/kg ONCE daily. Reduced, not contraindicated (GT7 Q109).

drill.q: Urgent CABG: how long before do you stop eptifibatide? Ticagrelor?
drill.a: Eptifibatide/tirofiban 2-4 h (GT7 Q116). Ticagrelor or clopidogrel ≥24 h. Elective: ticagrelor 3, clopidogrel 5, prasugrel 7 days.

drill.q: NSTE-ACS angiography timing: very high risk, high risk?
drill.a: Very high risk (shock, refractory pain, acute HF, arrhythmia): <2 h, class I. High risk (NSTEMI, GRACE >140, dynamic ST-T): <24 h, now IIa.

drill.q: GRACE vs TIMI: what does each predict, and which counts aspirin use?
drill.a: GRACE: death (>140 high risk). TIMI: death/MI/urgent revascularisation at 14 days; aspirin in the last 7 days adds a point.

drill.q: VT or NSVT 48 h after a large MI: mechanism? And sustained VT 2 years later?
drill.a: Abnormal automaticity at 24-72 h. Scar re-entry weeks to years later. AIVR = enhanced normal automaticity, benign.

drill.q: Complete heart block after anterior MI: level, escape, treatment?
drill.a: Infranodal (His-Purkinje), wide escape <40/min, atropine-resistant: transvenous pacing. Inferior MI: nodal, narrow escape, usually transient.

drill.q: Killip classes?
drill.a: I no HF; II S3 or crackles <50% of lung fields; III frank pulmonary oedema; IV cardiogenic shock.

drill.q: Inferior STEMI, new murmur, pulmonary oedema, cold and hypotensive: which intervention next?
drill.a: IABP (IIa for mechanical complications; lowers afterload), then surgery. Not norepinephrine (38% right). Routine IABP in shock is class III.

drill.q: Sudden PEA with tamponade days after a large STEMI?
drill.a: LV free wall rupture.

drill.q: ST elevation still present 6 weeks after anterior MI, Q waves, no troponin rise?
drill.a: LV aneurysm. Risk: apical thrombus → anticoagulate.

drill.q: After MI with EF 32%: which long-term drugs are class I?
drill.a: ACE inhibitor (GT8 Q26) and β-blocker; MRA if HF or diabetes; statin and 12-month DAPT for all. Not milrinone, digoxin or nitrates.

traps.trap: Most pre-hospital STEMI deaths are from cardiogenic shock or rupture
traps.truth: They are from VF, mostly in the first hour. Pump failure and rupture kill over the following days.

traps.trap: Low-flow nasal oxygen at 2 L/min is harmless at SaO₂ 95%
traps.truth: Routine oxygen at SaO₂ ≥90% is class III. Withhold it; oxygen only below 90% (PaO₂ <60 mmHg).

traps.trap: Morphine is a class I part of the ACS bundle
traps.truth: IIa only: it delays absorption of oral P2Y12 inhibitors.

traps.trap: Hypotension 10 min after nitroglycerin in inferior STEMI = medication reaction
traps.truth: The nitrate unmasked a preload-dependent RV infarct: cardiogenic shock. Check V4R before nitrates; treat with fluid.

traps.trap: Only PDE-5 inhibitors interact with nitrates
traps.truth: Riociguat (sGC stimulator) acts on the same NO-cGMP pathway and is also a contraindication.

traps.trap: Pain relieved by nitroglycerin + normal ECG + one negative troponin = oesophageal spasm
traps.truth: Nitrate relief proves nothing. DocT keys spasm; pick spasm only if serial troponins have excluded ACS, otherwise unstable angina.

traps.trap: The only contraindications to an IV β-blocker in STEMI are heart failure and hypotension
traps.truth: Also PR >240 ms or 2nd/3rd-degree block, active asthma, and shock risk (age >70, HR >110, SBP <120). The 'all except' key is 'none of the above'.

traps.trap: Transfer for primary PCI when the centre is 150 km / 4 h away, or door-to-balloon is 160 min
traps.truth: Beyond 120 min from diagnosis to wire: lyse within 10 min, then transfer.

traps.trap: 90 minutes is the cut-off for choosing PCI over lysis
traps.truth: 120 min is the choice. 60 min (PCI centre) and 90 min (transferred) are targets once PCI is chosen.

traps.trap: IV nitroglycerin, observation or echo first for new ST elevation after a stent
traps.truth: Acute stent thrombosis is a STEMI: urgent repeat angiography / PCI.

traps.trap: Thrombolysis for stent thrombosis
traps.truth: Platelet-rich stent thrombus responds poorly to lysis: DAPT, anticoagulation and urgent PCI.

traps.trap: Angiography 1 h or 48 h after successful lysis
traps.truth: 2-24 h (Marrow says 3-24 h). The mini-test answer was 12 h.

traps.trap: Lysis is effective from 2 to 24 hours
traps.truth: Lysis is for symptoms ≤12 h (best ≤2 h). 2-24 h is the angiography window after successful lysis.

traps.trap: Ticagrelor or prasugrel with tenecteplase; full-dose tenecteplase at 80 years
traps.truth: Clopidogrel is the P2Y12 inhibitor with lysis (300 mg; 75 mg if >75 y). Tenecteplase is halved at ≥75 y.

traps.trap: SBP >180 mmHg, or warfarin with aspirin, as an absolute contraindication to lysis
traps.truth: Both are relative. Previous haemorrhagic stroke is absolute, at any time.

traps.trap: Choosing 'ischaemic stroke 5 months ago' or 'surgery 2 weeks ago' over a known AVM
traps.truth: All are absolute on the ESC list, but the key is AVM: absolute in every guideline (ACC/AHA uses 3 months for stroke).

traps.trap: Massive PE, ischaemic stroke 2 months ago: lysis contraindicated only if anticoagulated
traps.truth: Ischaemic stroke within 6 months is an absolute contraindication (ESC).

traps.trap: Tirofiban or eptifibatide as the IV bridge for a stented patient who must stop clopidogrel
traps.truth: They block GP IIb/IIIa, not P2Y12. Cangrelor is the only IV P2Y12 inhibitor (BRIDGE).

traps.trap: Aspirin inhibits COX-1 reversibly
traps.truth: Irreversible acetylation: the effect lasts the platelet's life (7-10 days); urgent reversal needs platelet transfusion.

traps.trap: Aspirin or metoprolol blamed for dyspnoea 12 h after PCI with normal SpO₂, exam, ECG and CT
traps.truth: Ticagrelor (adenosine reuptake block); usually mild and self-limiting.

traps.trap: Clopidogrel, ticagrelor or cangrelor is the P2Y12 inhibitor contraindicated after a TIA
traps.truth: Only prasugrel is contraindicated after stroke or TIA (TRITON-TIMI 38).

traps.trap: Pretreat an NSTEMI with prasugrel before the coronary anatomy is known
traps.truth: Routine P2Y12 pretreatment in NSTE-ACS with early angiography planned is class III (ESC 2023; ACCOAST, ISAR-REACT 5). Defer to PCI.

traps.trap: Enoxaparin is contraindicated in NSTE-ACS with CrCl 24 mL/min
traps.truth: Reduce it: 1 mg/kg once daily when CrCl <30. UFH needs no adjustment; fondaparinux is the drug to avoid at low eGFR.

traps.trap: UFH is superior to enoxaparin / enoxaparin is contraindicated before an invasive strategy
traps.truth: Neither. The true statement is that fondaparinux causes less major bleeding than enoxaparin (OASIS-5).

traps.trap: Fondaparinux is a good sole anticoagulant for primary PCI
traps.truth: Class III (catheter thrombosis, OASIS-6). It is class I in NSTE-ACS with angiography >24 h away.

traps.trap: Enoxaparin or UFH as the best anticoagulant in STEMI with no reperfusion
traps.truth: Fondaparinux (OASIS-6).

traps.trap: A single troponin above the 99th percentile in CKD stage 4 = MI
traps.truth: Troponin is chronically raised; a rise and/or fall is required (Fourth Universal Definition).

traps.trap: ACC/AHA 2025: after 1 month of DAPT, continue aspirin alone
traps.truth: The class 1 option drops aspirin and continues ticagrelor monotherapy from ≥1 month after PCI.

traps.trap: Early invasive strategy within 24 h is class I in high-risk NSTE-ACS
traps.truth: ESC 2023 downgraded it to IIa. Class I: <2 h for very high risk, and an invasive strategy during the admission.

traps.trap: GRACE predicts 14-day events / aspirin use lowers the TIMI score
traps.truth: GRACE predicts death (>140 = high risk). TIMI predicts death, MI or urgent revascularisation at 14 days, and aspirin in the last 7 days ADDS a point.

traps.trap: Retroperitoneal bleed after a radial PCI
traps.truth: That belongs to femoral access (back pain, hypotension, non-contrast CT). After radial PCI with an unchanged ECG, think tamponade: bedside echo.

traps.trap: Stop eptifibatide 24 h before urgent CABG
traps.truth: Eptifibatide and tirofiban: 2-4 h. Abciximab ≥12 h.

traps.trap: Continue ticagrelor until surgery, or stop it 2-4 h before urgent CABG
traps.truth: Stop ticagrelor or clopidogrel ≥24 h before urgent CABG (elective: ticagrelor 3, clopidogrel 5, prasugrel 7 days). Aspirin continues.

traps.trap: Complete revascularisation at the index procedure in cardiogenic shock
traps.truth: Culprit-only (CULPRIT-SHOCK); complete revascularisation is for the stable patient.

traps.trap: Re-entry (or enhanced normal automaticity, or afterdepolarisations) for VT / NSVT 48 h after MI
traps.truth: Abnormal automaticity at 24-72 h. Re-entry is for early VF and for scar VT weeks to years later; enhanced normal automaticity is AIVR.

traps.trap: Treat AIVR with amiodarone or lidocaine
traps.truth: Benign reperfusion rhythm; suppressing it can leave asystole.

traps.trap: Anterior MI most commonly produces 2nd- and 3rd-degree AV block
traps.truth: Inferior MI causes more block of every degree. Keyed true statement: AV block develops transiently in 10-25% of acute MIs.

traps.trap: DocT key: block after ANTERIOR MI is Mobitz I, benign, resolves with atropine
traps.truth: Wrong key. Anterior MI block is infranodal (His-Purkinje), wide escape, atropine-resistant: transvenous pacing.

traps.trap: Loop diuretic and wait, intubation, hydralazine or labetalol for hypertensive pulmonary oedema
traps.truth: High-dose IV nitroglycerin + NIV first (taught in Shock II).

traps.trap: Dopamine as the first vasopressor in post-MI cardiogenic shock
traps.truth: Norepinephrine (SOAP II). An older DocT QBank key still says dopamine.
traps.asked: DocT GT, 76% right; DocT QBank old key 38%

traps.trap: Routine IABP in STEMI cardiogenic shock; lysis when PCI is 75 min away
traps.truth: Routine IABP is class III (IABP-SHOCK II); IIa only for mechanical complications. Within 120 min, primary PCI.

traps.trap: Lyse a STEMI in cardiogenic shock because the PCI centre is 3.5 h away
traps.truth: Shock: transfer for revascularisation whatever the delay (ESC allows lysis as a bridge, IIa, if >120 min and no mechanical complication).

traps.trap: Milrinone, dobutamine or epinephrine for low output on a chronic β-blocker when levosimendan is offered
traps.truth: Levosimendan is the exam key; milrinone if levosimendan is not offered (taught in Shock II).

traps.trap: β1 stimulation or troponin C sensitisation for the drug that raises CO, venodilates and speeds SR calcium reuptake
traps.truth: PDE-3 inhibition (milrinone): cAMP rises below the receptor.

traps.trap: Norepinephrine for shock with a new murmur and pulmonary oedema after inferior STEMI
traps.truth: IABP: lowers afterload and the regurgitant/shunt fraction as a bridge to surgery (IIa). A pressor worsens the leak.

traps.trap: Valve replacement as the NEXT step for papillary rupture when IABP is offered; or diuretics/vasodilator and wait when it is not
traps.truth: 'Next' with IABP offered: IABP (44% right). No IABP option: urgent mitral surgery (62% right). Never medical therapy alone.

traps.trap: PE or LV systolic dysfunction for dyspnoea with a new apical holosystolic murmur after posterior MI
traps.truth: Acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle dysfunction/rupture.

traps.trap: Acute coronary syndrome for Q waves in I, aVL, V5 without ST change; re-infarction for ST elevation persisting weeks after anterior MI
traps.truth: Q waves alone = old MI. Persistent ST elevation + Q waves, no troponin rise = LV aneurysm.

traps.trap: Missing the ACE inhibitor as long-term therapy after MI with EF 32%
traps.truth: ACE inhibitor is class I at LVEF ≤40% (anti-remodelling), with a β-blocker, and an MRA if HF or diabetes.

traps.trap: IV milrinone, digoxin or nitrates to improve prognosis after MI with EF 25%
traps.truth: Oral β-blocker (prognostic). Inotropes worsen long-term survival; digoxin and nitrates treat symptoms.

traps.trap: A long-term β-blocker improves outcome in every post-MI patient
traps.truth: Proven at LVEF ≤40%, pooled benefit at 40-49%, none shown at ≥50% (REDUCE-AMI, REBOOT).

traps.trap: LDL-C 60 mg/dL on maximal statin: adding ezetimibe is class 1; restrictive transfusion (Hb 7) in acute MI
traps.truth: Class 1 starts at LDL-C ≥70 (55-69 is 2a). In ACS with anaemia, Hb 10 may be reasonable (2b, MINT).

mimics.pair: Early death vs later death in STEMI
mimics.tell: First hour: VF (electrical). Days later: pump failure and rupture (mechanical).

mimics.pair: Nitrate in hypertensive pulmonary oedema vs in RV infarct
mimics.tell: Lowering preload rescues the congested LV and collapses the preload-dependent RV.

mimics.pair: Tachycardia of pain vs tachycardia of low output
mimics.tell: The first is a β-blocker target; the second is holding the output up, and blocking it causes shock (COMMIT).

mimics.pair: 120 min vs 90 min
mimics.tell: 120 is the decision threshold between PCI and lysis; 90 is the target for a transferred patient.

mimics.pair: Rescue PCI vs routine (pharmaco-invasive) PCI vs facilitated PCI
mimics.tell: Rescue: lysis failed, go now. Routine: lysis worked, 2-24 h. Facilitated (immediate PCI after full lysis): not recommended.

mimics.pair: Stent thrombosis vs post-PCI chest pain
mimics.tell: New ST elevation in the stented territory = stent thrombosis, back to the lab. Unchanged ECG gives time.

mimics.pair: Lysis window vs post-lysis angiography window
mimics.tell: Lysis: symptoms ≤12 h. Angiography: 2-24 h after a successful lytic.

mimics.pair: P2Y12 inhibitor with lysis vs with PCI
mimics.tell: Lysis: clopidogrel. PCI: prasugrel or ticagrelor.

mimics.pair: Ischaemic stroke vs TIA within 6 months (lysis)
mimics.tell: Same window, different class: stroke absolute, TIA relative.

mimics.pair: Cangrelor vs eptifibatide/tirofiban
mimics.tell: Cangrelor blocks P2Y12 and replaces the oral drug; the others block GP IIb/IIIa and are bail-out drugs.

mimics.pair: Thienopyridines vs ticagrelor
mimics.tell: Clopidogrel and prasugrel are irreversible prodrugs; ticagrelor is direct-acting and reversible (and causes adenosine dyspnoea).

mimics.pair: Ticagrelor dyspnoea vs PE or heart failure after PCI
mimics.tell: Ticagrelor: SpO₂, examination, ECG and CT all normal.

mimics.pair: Fondaparinux class I vs class III
mimics.tell: Class I in NSTE-ACS with angiography >24 h away; class III as the sole anticoagulant in primary PCI (catheter thrombosis).

mimics.pair: Enoxaparin vs fondaparinux vs UFH in renal failure
mimics.tell: Enoxaparin: once daily below CrCl 30. Fondaparinux: avoid at low eGFR. UFH: no change.

mimics.pair: ESC 2023 vs ACC/AHA 2025 at the end of DAPT
mimics.tell: ESC: 12 months by default (IIa: single antiplatelet, preferably the P2Y12 inhibitor, after 3–6 months if event-free and not high ischaemic risk). ACC/AHA: can drop aspirin at 1 month and continue ticagrelor alone.

mimics.pair: Very high-risk NSTE-ACS vs STEMI
mimics.tell: Both reach the lab within 2 h, but NSTE-ACS is never lysed.

mimics.pair: GRACE vs TIMI (UA/NSTEMI)
mimics.tell: GRACE: weighted, predicts death. TIMI: seven one-point items, 14-day composite; only TIMI counts aspirin use.

mimics.pair: Hypotension after femoral PCI vs after radial PCI
mimics.tell: Femoral + back pain: retroperitoneal bleed (CT). Radial + unchanged ECG: tamponade (echo).

mimics.pair: GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor vs oral P2Y12 inhibitor before CABG
mimics.tell: Eptifibatide/tirofiban: hours (2-4). Oral P2Y12 inhibitors: a day to a week.

mimics.pair: Stable multivessel ACS vs multivessel ACS in shock
mimics.tell: Stable: complete revascularisation, index or staged. Shock: culprit only.

mimics.pair: AIVR vs VT
mimics.tell: AIVR runs near the sinus rate and comes and goes with it; VT is faster and sustained.

mimics.pair: Enhanced normal vs abnormal automaticity
mimics.tell: Normal: a pacemaker cell firing faster (AIVR). Abnormal: an injured non-pacemaker cell firing on its own (VT at 24-72 h).

mimics.pair: AV block after inferior vs anterior MI
mimics.tell: Inferior: nodal, narrow escape 40-60, atropine works, transient. Anterior: infranodal, wide escape <40, needs pacing.

mimics.pair: Mobitz I vs Mobitz II after MI
mimics.tell: Mobitz I (PR lengthens) is nodal and benign; Mobitz II (fixed PR, sudden dropped beat) is infranodal and needs pacing.

mimics.pair: Shock from pump failure vs from a mechanical complication
mimics.tell: Pump failure: PCI, no routine IABP. New murmur or tamponade: IABP is IIa as a bridge to surgery.

mimics.pair: RV infarct vs LV cardiogenic shock
mimics.tell: RV: clear lungs, raised JVP, give fluid. LV: crackles, avoid fluid.

mimics.pair: VSR vs papillary muscle rupture
mimics.tell: VSR: loud murmur with thrill at the left sternal edge, O₂ step-up. Papillary: apical, often soft murmur, flash pulmonary oedema.

mimics.pair: Apical vs basal VSR
mimics.tell: Apical follows anterior MI and is simpler; basal follows inferior MI, is complex and does worse.

mimics.pair: True aneurysm vs pseudoaneurysm
mimics.tell: True: wide neck, scar wall, rarely ruptures. Pseudo: narrow neck, contained rupture walled by pericardium, needs surgery.

mimics.pair: Old MI vs acute MI vs aneurysm on ECG
mimics.tell: Q waves alone: old. ST elevation with symptoms/troponin: acute. Q waves with ST elevation persisting for weeks: aneurysm.

mimics.pair: Hb threshold: ACS vs general ICU
mimics.tell: ACS with anaemia: Hb 10 may be reasonable (MINT). General ICU: 7.

new_cards.q:

a Enoxaparin: the usual NSTE-ACS dose
b Enoxaparin when CrCl is <30 mL/min, and the floor
c Why it accumulates
d Fondaparinux
e UFH and bivalirudin
f The age rule for enoxaparin with fibrinolysis
a: CrCl **<30 mL/min → 1 mg/kg ONCE daily** (reduced, **not contraindicated**); ESC: not recommended if eGFR <15
Short heparin chains are **renally cleared** → anti-Xa effect accumulates → bleeding
Fondaparinux 2.5 mg daily: **avoid if eGFR <20** (ESC; product label: CrCl <30)
**UFH: no renal adjustment** (the fallback in severe renal failure); bivalirudin: reduce the infusion if CrCl <30
With fibrinolysis at **≥75 y**: no IV bolus, **0.75 mg/kg** every 12 h
Trap: 'enoxaparin is contraindicated' at CrCl 24. The key is 1 mg/kg once daily
new_cards.why: GT7 Q109 (missed: chose 'contraindicated', key enoxaparin 1 mg/kg once daily at CrCl 24). No card in the pack gives renal dosing of the anticoagulants.

new_cards.topic: Post-MI ventricular arrhythmias: mechanism by timing
new_cards.q:
**Give the mechanism of ventricular arrhythmia after MI by its timing:**
a First minutes to hours (early VF)
b At reperfusion (AIVR)
c 24-72 h (PVCs, NSVT, VT)
d Weeks to years (sustained monomorphic VT)
e Where afterdepolarisations belong
a: Minutes-hours: **re-entry** in acutely ischaemic myocardium → early VF
Reperfusion: **enhanced NORMAL automaticity** of Purkinje pacemaker cells → AIVR (benign)
**24-72 h: ABNORMAL automaticity** in partially depolarised surviving Purkinje fibres and myocytes; driven by catecholamines, low K⁺ / Mg²⁺
Early afterdepolarisations: long QT / torsades. Delayed afterdepolarisations: digoxin, Ca²⁺ overload. Neither is the post-MI answer
Trap: 're-entry' for VT or NSVT at 48 h. Choose re-entry only when the stem is weeks to years after the MI
new_cards.why: DocT GT ×4 (VT 48 h after a large anterior MI ×2, 83-87% right; stable NSVT 48 h after MI ×2, 61-67% right): key abnormal automaticity. MI-58 gives only the AIVR mechanism and the management.

card_flags.issue: Part d lists only heart failure and hypotension as IV β-blocker contraindications. Marrow's 'all except' question also counts PR >240 ms or 2nd/3rd-degree block, active asthma/bronchospasm and high shock risk (age >70, HR >110, SBP <120; COMMIT). Suggest adding them.
Contraindication list omits riociguat (sGC stimulator), which Marrow keyed, and the PDE-5 windows (sildenafil/vardenafil 24 h, tadalafil 48 h; these are on CAR-20). Suggest one added line.
Ticagrelor dyspnoea (adenosine, ~14% in PLATO, normal SpO₂/exam/ECG/CT) is not on the card but was a DocT GT question with 30% correct. Suggest adding to part d.

Card has no pre-CABG stop times, asked twice in DocT GT (GT7 Q116: eptifibatide/tirofiban 2-4 h; ticagrelor/clopidogrel ≥24 h before urgent CABG; elective 3/5/7 days for ticagrelor/clopidogrel/prasugrel). Taught in the lesson; suggest adding a line.
Card gives only the AIVR mechanism; the 24-72 h 'abnormal automaticity' answer (DocT GT ×4) is absent. Covered by new card V12-011.

Table implies 3rd-degree block is only 'distal/LAD'. Inferior MI also causes complete block (nodal, narrow escape, usually transient) and causes more block of every degree than anterior MI. Mobitz II is missing from the distal column. Also the DocT GT key 'Mobitz I, benign, atropine' for block after ANTERIOR MI contradicts its own explanation.
Killip classification (Marrow question) is not on the card; taught in the lesson.

Part d answers milrinone for the patient on carvedilol; DocT GT keys levosimendan (GT7 Q87, GT8 Q82, both missed). Suggest 'levosimendan (exam key) or milrinone', matching V12-003. Part a 'whatever the delay': ESC 2023 also allows lysis (IIa, C) if PPCI >120 min away and no mechanical complication.

VSR 'early surgery 20-40%' mortality is optimistic: STS registry operative mortality about 54% when repaired within 7 days of MI, 18% after 7 days. Free wall and papillary figures left as on the card.
Part a says 'anterior or posterolateral MI (per notes)'; the standard pairing is anterior (apical defect) and inferior (basal defect, worse prognosis). Part b mortality 20-40% is low, as for MI-64.

'Long-term oral anticoagulation' for LV thrombus: ESC 2023 says OAC should be considered for 3-6 months, guided by repeat imaging (IIa, C). The lesson teaches the card's wording as the classic key and the guideline as current.
MRA is graded I, B on the card; ESC 2023 gives I, A (LVEF ≤40% with HF or diabetes). The card says 'LVEF ≤40% AND HF' and omits diabetes.

Part f calls transfer to shock centres 'Class 1'. I could not confirm a classed recommendation for this in the 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline text (the pack's own explanation says the same); the hub-and-spoke statement appears in the ACC 2025 concise guidance on cardiogenic shock, which carries no class. Lesson teaches the idea without the grade.

'Door-to-needle ≤30 min' is the older ACCF/AHA 2013 figure beside the ESC ≤10 min from diagnosis; 'mini test: 3-24 h' vs ESC 2-24 h. Both are flagged in the lesson; no change needed if the card keeps both.
